answer_text:
Great question! Computing square roots is actually one of the most fascinating problems in computer science, and there are several clever methods used. Here's a thorough breakdown:

---

## How Computers and Calculators Compute Square Roots

### The Core Idea: Iterative Methods

There are many ways to calculate the square root, but they all share a common property: they start with an initial guess and then refine that guess over many steps. These are called **iterative methods**.

The idea is simple: checking whether a number *x* is the square root of *a* is very easy — just multiply it by itself and you can estimate the error |a − x²|. You then know whether you need to increase or decrease your guess. You do this many times and the accuracy of your guess constantly improves.

---

### Method 1: The Babylonian / Newton-Raphson Method

This is arguably the most famous and widely used approach.

The iterative method is called the **Babylonian method** for finding square roots, or sometimes Hero's method. It was known to the ancient Babylonians (1500 BC) and Greeks (100 AD) long before Newton invented his general procedure.

To calculate √p, you choose any initial value as your first guess *x*, then iterate. If *x* is greater than √p, then p/x will be smaller than √p — meaning *x* and p/x *bracket* the value you want to find. You can then take their average to get a better approximation, closer to the true root.

The formula looks like this:

> **x_new = (x + S/x) / 2**

You keep iterating — applying the formula x_(n+1) = (x_n + S/x_n) / 2 — until the process converges. Convergence is achieved when the digits of x_(n+1) and x_n agree to as many decimal places as you desire.

It turns out that this Babylonian square-root algorithm is a special case of **Newton's general method** for finding the roots of functions. To see this, define the function f(x) = x² - S. Notice that the square root of S is the positive root of f.

By performing this iteration, it is possible to evaluate a square root to any desired accuracy by only using the basic arithmetic operations.

---

### Method 2: The Fast Inverse Square Root (and the "Magic Constant" Trick)

Modern processors often compute **1/√a** (the *reciprocal* square root) rather than √a directly, for a clever reason:

Modern processors can calculate additions and multiplications very fast, almost at the same speed. But divisions are difficult and much slower. Consequently, if a square root calculation algorithm uses division, it will be slow too.

A clever trick removes all divisions: calculate **1/√a** instead of √a! Once you have 1/√a, you simply multiply it by *a* to get √a.

A famous example of this is the **Fast Inverse Square Root** algorithm:

The key of the fast inverse square root was to directly compute an approximation by utilizing the structure of floating-point numbers, proving faster than table lookups. The algorithm was approximately four times faster than computing the square root with another method and calculating the reciprocal via floating-point division.

The trick came from treating the 32-bit floating-point word as an integer, then subtracting it from a "magic constant," **0x5F3759DF**. This produces a surprisingly good initial estimate, which is then refined with one or two Newton-Raphson iterations.

---

### Method 3: Lookup Tables as a Starting Point

The duration of execution of most square root algorithms is directly related to the precision of the *starting estimate*. Depending on the accuracy of this "seed" value, the algorithm will require fewer or more iterations to arrive at the result with the desired precision.

Many platforms implement square root functions using **direct lookup tables** or **polynomial approximations**, with a subsequent application of the Newton–Raphson method. Essentially, the hardware looks up a rough answer in a pre-computed table and then polishes it with iteration.

Tabular methods are very fast but require a large area (memory), since the size of the table grows exponentially with an increase in required precision. This may pose a problem not only for small devices such as microcontrollers, but also FPGAs.

---

### Method 4: Dedicated Hardware Instructions

Hardware manufacturers have added dedicated instructions that make many of these software tricks redundant. For example, on x86, Intel introduced the SSE instruction `rsqrtss` in 1999. Modern CPUs have specialized arithmetic units that can compute square roots directly in hardware in just a few clock cycles.

---

### Why Is It So Accurate?

The magic lies in how *quickly* these iterative methods converge. Newton's method in particular exhibits **quadratic convergence** — meaning the number of correct decimal digits roughly *doubles* with every iteration. So after just 5–10 iterations from a reasonable starting guess, a computer can have an answer accurate to dozens of decimal places — far more than what any screen or application could ever display.

In short, computers don't "know" the square root — they make a smart guess and rapidly close in on the right answer using elegant mathematics developed over thousands of years!
